metadata.notes: Attack path derived from Mandiant M-Trends 2026 'The Cascading Impact of Third-Party SaaS Compromises' (pp. 74-77). UNC5221-style pattern: compromise a SaaS provider via a public-facing webshell / SQLi, extract Azure Service Principals and OAuth refresh tokens, then present them in downstream customer tenants. Sources: M-Trends 2026 pp. 21, 74-77. History: v2.5 recorded the provider-to-customer segment as #4 -> #10; the v2.6 requalification (2026-09-23) re-sequenced it to #10 -> #4, reading the stolen service-principal secret as subverted federation trust material. Correction (2026-11-10): the #10 step is removed. A service-principal secret is a credential of the provider's application, not trust material of the identity provider; the identity provider was not subverted and issued its tokens correctly, so the customer tenant honouring them is the trust link working as designed and is not a step (core §4 #10, federation test; whitepaper B19: stolen credentials at an identity provider that was not subverted give #4 -> #1). Falsifiability: leave the secret with the attacker and remove the provider compromise, and the entry into the customer still succeeds, so it was never #10. The crossing into the customer is #4 with its boundary annotated. Step ids renumbered (s5 = #4, s6 = #1). Path: #2 -> #7 -> #1 -> #1 + [DRE: C] -> #4 -> #1 + [DRE: C].

path_sequence.notes: Exploitation of the SaaS provider's internet-facing admin/API plane: SQL injection, deserialization, or webshell upload via an authenticated admin app. R-ROLE: the SaaS provider's application is in server role relative to the attacker → #2 (Exploiting Server).

Webshell / post-exploitation implant installed on the provider's infrastructure. R-EXEC satisfied: FEC execution of attacker-supplied code on the provider's server. Enables persistent hands-on-keyboard operations inside the provider's tenancy.

Azure AD / Entra ID reconnaissance within the provider's tenant: enumerate service principals, OAuth applications, and multi-tenant integrations. Legitimate cloud management APIs, abused scope. No exploit, no FEC.

Extract service-principal secrets / OAuth refresh tokens that grant the provider's app delegated access into downstream customer tenants. Legitimate secret-retrieval APIs (Key Vault, configuration store), abused scope. DRE:C — the provider's cross-tenant credentials are the crown jewels.

Authentication into the downstream customer tenant using the exfiltrated service-principal secret. R-CRED / Axiom X: credential application is ALWAYS #4, regardless of how the credential was acquired. The authentication looks indistinguishable from normal provider-to-customer integration traffic. This is the crossing into the customer: an internal cluster crossing a domain boundary, annotated ||[auth][@External→@Customer]||. No #10 precedes it: the identity provider that issued the token was not subverted, and the customer tenant honouring that token is the trust link working as designed (core §4 #10, federation test).

Use of delegated API access to query customer data (CRM records, documents, emails). Legitimate, audited API calls — abused scope. DRE:C. The downstream victim's only observable signal is behavioral: unusual query volume or off-hours access from the provider's service principal.
